Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC.( 1980) 60, 263-281
Lower Cretaceous magnetic stratigraphy in
Umbrian pelagic carbonate rocks
wifiam bW rie
Institut fur Geophysik, ETH Honggerberg, CH-8093
Zurich, Switzerland
Walter AhareZ
Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of California,
Berkeley, California 94 720, USA
Isabella Premoli Silva
Istituto di Paleontologia, university ofMilan,
Milan, Italy
Sbonett a Monechi
Istituto di Geologia, University ojFlorence,
Florence, Ital-v
Received 1979 June 22; in original form 1979 May 17
Summary. A record of geomagnetic field polarity for the Barremian, Aptian
and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous has been derived in three over-
lapping sections of pelagic carbonate rocks in the Umbrian Apennines of
northern Italy. The remanence carrier in the greyish-white Majolica limestone
and Fucoid Marls is magnetite, with haematite also an important constituent
in a zone of ‘couches rouges’ within the Fucoid Marls. The weak remanent
magnetizations were measured with a cryogenic magnetometer. Alternating
field or thermal demagnetization was used to isolate the characteristic remanent
magnetization (ChRM) in 655 specimens from 248 stratigraphic levels. The
samples respond positively to a tectonic fold test, indicating that the ChRM
predates the Late Tertiary folding of the Umbrian sequence. The magnetic
stratigraphy derived from variations of virtual geomagnetic pole latitude
clearly defines the recognizable reversal pattern associated with Mesozoic
marine magnetic anomalies MO to M4. The sections have been zones palaeon-
tologically on the basis of planktonic foraminifera and calcareous nannofossil
assemblages. The ages of magnetic anomalies MO to M4 determined in this
way are somewhat older than those in the reversal time scale of Larson &
Hilde (1975). Anomaly MO is located in the Early Aptian, close to the Aptian/
Barremian boundary. A long period of normal polarity in the Aptian and
Albian corresponds to the early part of the Cretaceous magnetic quiet zone.
It is interrupted in the Late Aptian by a reversal which we fmd in only one of
the Fucoid Marl sections, and which has not been reported in oceanic
magnetic anomaly investigations.

### page_2
264 W. Lowrie et al.
1 Introduction
The record of geomagnetic polarity during the Mesozoic and Cenozoic is known best from
interpretation of the magnetic anomaly lineations recorded in oceanic crust formed during
this time, since the break-up of Pangaea in the Late Triassic. The largest part of this polarity
record has not yet been confirmed by independent palaeomagnetic investigations. The
youngest portion of the magnetic time scale of Heirtzler et al. (1968) correlates excellently
with the polarity sequence determined in radiometrically dated lavas younger than about
3.5 Myr (Doell, Dalrymple & Cox 1966). The older Cenozoic and Late Cretaceous anomalies
were dated by simple linear extrapolation from this short baseline. Although McDougalletaZ.
(1977) have extended recently the baseline length to about 6.5 Myr in stratigraphically
sequential lavas, the geomagnetic polarity record for the remainder of the Cenozoic has not
yet been verified. For most of this period the errors inherent in radiometric dating prohibit
development of a magnetic reversal sequence from stratigraphically unrelated samples. On
the other hand recent major improvements in magnetometer technology now permit rapid
and accurate investigation of sedimentary sequences whose remanent magnetizations were
previously measurable only with great difficulty or not at all. Particularly well suited for
magnetic stratigraphy studies are sequences of pelagic carbonate rocks.
The sequence of geomagnetic reversals derived from the Late Cretaceous anomalies 34 to
29 has been confirmed recently in the Scaglia Rossa pelagic limestone at Gubbio in the
Northern Apennines of Italy (Lowrie & Alvarez 1977a,b) and verified in a nearby check
section at Moria (Fig. 1) (Alvarez & Lowrie 1978). The reversals were correlated to the
Campanian and Maastrichtian stages by palaeontological zonation of the Gubbio section
(Premoli Silva 1977) which has been established as a magnetostratigraphic type section for
the Late Cretaceous (Alvarez et al. 1977). The Gubbio and Moria sections also confirmed the
existence of a long period of normal geomagnetic polarity preceding anomaly 34 which
could be correlated with the Cretaceous magnetic quiet zone.
According to the oceanic anomaly record the onset of the Cretaceous quiet interval marks
the termination of the Mesozoic reversal sequence (Larsor. & Pitman 1972). The youngest
anomaly of this sequence is designated MO and has been assigned a Late Aptian age (Larson
& Hilde 1975). Recent magnetic stratigraphy studies ir, the Southern (Vicentinian) Alps by
Channell, Lowrie & Medizza (1979) have cast doubt on this date. They derived a magnetic
stratigraphy in the Early Cretaceous Biancone limestone, in which MO was dated at the base
of the Aptian.
The present investigation was undertaken to confirm and date the youngest reversals of
the Mesozoic sequence, in particular to determine the age of anomaly MO. These new studies
have been carried out in three partially overlapping sections of pelagic carbonate rocks at
Poggio le Guaine, Valdorbia and Gorgo a Cerbara in the Umbrian Apennines of northern
Italy (Fig. 1). Data from a single site in the Valdorbia section were incorporated in a compo-
site polar wander path for Umbria by VandenBerg, Klootwijk &Wonders (1978). This Late
Aptian site was reversely magnetized, but we will show that this Valdorbia reversal does not
correspond to anomaly MO.
2 Lithostratigraphy and sampling scheme
In the Umbrian sequence the Late Cretaceous is represented by the greyish-white, Ceno-
manian to mid-Turonian, Scaglia Rianca limestone and the pink-to-red Scaglia Rossa lime-
stone which extends from the mid-Turonian through the remaining Late Cretaceous stages
and, indeed, was deposited until the Middle Eocene. The magnetic stratigraphy of these
pelagic limestones was developed and checked in the Gubbio and Moria sections (Lowrie &
Alvarez 1977a, b; Alvarez 8i Lowrie 1978).

Figure 1. Location map of the northern Umbrian Apennines. The Lower Cretaceous pelagic carbonate
sediments for the present study were sampled from the sections at Gorgo a Cerbara, Poggio le Guiane and
Valdorbia. The magnetic stratigraphy of the Upper Cretaceous was determined in earlier studies of lime-
stone sections at Gubbio and Moria.
Late Aptian and Albian stages are represented in the Umbrian sequence by marls, with
bedding planes occasionally marked by fucoids (‘Scisti a Fucoidi’). These Fucoid Marls con-
sist of an upper grey member and a lower red member (‘couches rouges’), both of which are
characterized by indurated beds from a few centimetres to about 15 cm in thickness,
separated by marly intervals that can be up to a few metres thick, and which can only rarely
be sampled. The Fucoid Marls were sampled in overlapping sections at all three locations
(Fig. 2).
The Early Cretaceous stages up to and including the Early Aptian are represented in the
Umbrian sequence by the Majolica limestone, which is the lithologically-similar, Umbrian
equivalent of the Biancone limestone that was successfully investigated by Channel1 et al.
(1979) in the Southern Alps. It is a compact, white, pelagic limestone containing black chert

### page_5
Magnetic stratigraphy in carbonate rocks 267
beds, whose name derives from its porcelain-like appearance on fresh-broken surfaces (the
Majolica lacks the large planktonic foraminifera which cause the Scaglia to break on surfaces
speckled with little bumps). The Majolica limestone was sampled only in the Gorgo a
Cerbara section; frequent soft-sediment slumping and faulting disturb the Majolica in Umbria
and only at this location could we be sure of good control of these tectonic complications.
Preliminary sampling of the three sections was based on a combination of oriented hand
samples and drilled cores. Later, more intensive sampling was carried out by taking closely
spaced drilled cores in zones of particular interest. Only the indurated beds were sampled,
and as a result the sample distribution is somewhat irregular in the Fucoid Marls, although
where possible the sampling interval was kept to less than a metre.
2.1 THE POGGIO LE GUAINE SECTION
The Poggio le Guaine section is located on the flat-dipping, crestal part of an anticlinal
mountain near the town of Cagli (Fig. 1). Although the Scisti a Fucoidi and Scaglia are both
severely disturbed a short distance (0.5 km) to the northeast, the section itself is apparently
undisturbed. The Fucoid Marl beds are flat-lying and well-exposed, and could be sampled up
to the gradational transition into the overlying Scaglia Bianca; in this section faulting is
minor and compensatable. The Scaglia Bianca/Fucoid Marl contact is placed at the lowest
occurrence of chert nodules in the Scagha. The Fucoid Marls, which are free of chert,
continue downward through the middle and lower Albian into the upper Aptian. Sampling
of the section was terminated at the Fucoid Marl/Majolica contact. This contact is placed at
the highest occurrence of chert nodules in the Majolica, and falls in the upper Aptian. Fifty-
two beds were sampled, yielding 180 25-mm cylindrical palaeomagnetic specimens. The
underlying Majolica limestone at this location forms a precipitous cliff which was not
sampled because of the difficulty of access.
2.2 THE VALDORBIA SECTION
The Valdorbia section liesin a roadcut beside thc Scheggia- -Sassoferato road, 5 km northeast
of Scheggia (Fig. 1). The sampled interval covers only the lower part of the Fucoid Marls,
which are severely disturbed in their upper part; a fault of unknown throw is found in the
middle of the section. However, although it lies close to a syncline and thrust, the section is
continuous and undisturbed upward from the Majolica for 30 in into the Fucoid Marls, and
is defMtely not overturned. The ISEA reversed site of VandenBerg et al. (1978) is located in
this section. The beds dip fairly uniformly at about 55" to the south-west. A total of 24
oriented hand samples yielded 97 palaeomagnetic specimens. The underlying Majolica lime-
stone is also well-exposed here, but is covered by steel netting to prevent loose blocks from
falling on to the roadway.
2.3 THE GOKGO A CEKBAKA SECTION
The Gorgo a Cerbara section is located in the bed of the Candigliano River, 4 km east of the
town of Piobbico (Fig. 1). The upper grey member of the Fucoid Mark is intensely distorted
but the lower 'couches rouges' member and the Majolica lie in conformable contact with one
another and are excellently exposed, with a uniform dip of about 50" to the north-east. Thc
section is in fact on the flank of an anticline whose Early Jurassic core is exposed along the
river. Although the Majolica is well exposed in the stream bed for a thickness of several
hundred metres, synsedimentary slumping and subsequent faulting are common.

From 860 to 874m the section is cut by a fault. However, the offset could be determined
and allowed for by matching two distinctive slump beds, each about 1 m thick, across the
fault. Although the presence of slump beds indicated some penecontemporaneous disturbance
of the section, this appears to be minor, and it does not interrupt the continuity of the
nannoplankton zonation. At 842.5 m, we encountered a disturbed zone parallel to bedding;
since we could not be sure of continuity of section below this level, we terminated sampling
at this point. A total of 187 hand and drilled samples yielded 378 specimens from this
section.
2.4 SEDIMENTATION RATES AND SAMPLING INTERVAL
The sedimentation rates in the different sections were calculated by determining the thick-
ness of sediment deposited in each stage (whose boundary positions were determined
palaeontologically as described in the next section) and assigning to each stage boundary the
age given by Sigal (1977). The Albian and Upper Aptian Fucoid Marls at Poggio le Guaine
are about 70m thick, and span a time interval of some 12Myr. Their mean sedimentation
rate is around 6m Myr-'. The Lower Aptian and Barremian parts of the Majolica limestone
at Gorgo a Cerbara are about 60 m thick and represent some 10 Myr. Here again the mean
sedimentation rate is about 6m Myr-'. It should be noted that much higher sedimentation
rates (around 25 m Myr-') are necessary lower in the section to account for the tremendous
thickness of Majolica limestone extending to the Cretaceous-Jurassic boundary.
The average sedimentation rate of 6m Myr-' allows us to estimate approximately the
time intervals represented by our sampling. Within each standard one-inch specimen data are
averaged for up to 4000yr. In some parts of the sections the sampling interval was a few
centimetres, representing about 10 000 yr; in other stratigraphic intervals, particularly in
the marly grey member of the Fucoid Mark at Poggio le Guaine, the sampleable indurated
beds were occasionally as far as 3 m apart, a gap equivalent to about 500 000 yr. If reversals
of the geomagnetic field occurred during deposition of the few large marly gaps they may
have been missed in our sampling.
3. Palaeontological zonation
In the period of time corresponding to deposition of the Fucoid Mark (mainly Aptian-Albian)
planktonic foraminifera can be abundant and rich in diagnostic forms on whose distribution
a detailed zonation has been established (Sigal 1577;P remoli Silva, Paggi & Monechi 1976).
Earlier than the Aptian, planktonic foraminiferal assemblages are very rare, poorly diversified
and of little use for a detailed biostratigraphy. This is particularly true for facies such as the
Majolica. Calcareous nannoplankton are the best represented and the most useful fossils in
the Lower Cretaceous. Their biostratigraphic resolution is not very high (biozones are quite
comprehensive), however some appearances and extinctions within the calcareous nannofossil
assemblages correlate well with stage boundaries (Thierstein 1973).
In the present paper foraminifera were studied by Premoli Silva both on washed material
and in thin section, while calcareous nannoplankton were studied by Monechi with optical
and scanning electron microscopes. The planktonic foraminiferal and calcareous nannoplank-
ton biozenes identified in the three sections are plotted and correlated with stages in Fig. 2.
Planktonic foraminifera occur discontinuously throughout the Fucoid Mark due to heavy
dissolution in the middle and basal parts of the formation; some levels are completely
carbonate-free. Consequently some biozones could not be identified. Dissolution affected
the nannoplankton also; however, the phenomenon did not prevent identification of the
zones.

3.1 POGGIO LE GUAINE SECTION
In the Poggio le Guaine Section, the Scaglia Bianca/Fucoid Marls contact is placed at the
lowest occurrence of chert nodules. The hghest palaeontological sample came from 7 m below
this level and yielded a planktonic foraminiferal fauna belonging to the Ticinella breggiensis
Zone (T. praeticinensis Sub-zone) correlated with the lower part of the Upper Albian. The
remaining part of the Fucoid Mads is attributed to the Middle and Lower Albian and Upper
Aptian. The Albian/Aptian boundary is located on the basis of the appearance of the nanno-
lith Predicosphaera cretacea, whereas planktonic foraminifera are poorly represented,
The contact between Fucoid Maris and Majolica is placed at the highest occurrence of
chert nodules. On the basis again of the nannoplankton content, it falls in the Upper Aptian.
Planktonic foraminifera present in the basal part of the Fucoid Marls are poorly diagnostic.
3.2 VALDORBIA SECTION
The Valdorbia Section covers only the lower part of the Fucoid Marls. Planktonic foramini-
feral zones from the Lower and Upper Aptian and Middle Albian were recognized. Nanno-
fossils are not diagnostic in this section. A possible fault within the shaly interval at about
214m removes the latest Aptian, the Early Albian and part of the middle Albian. The faunal
change is very abrupt and leaves no doubt about the ages above and below the discontinuity.
The reversed polarity zone is located in indurated beds just below, but clear of, the fault.
We use the site designation ISEA of VandenBerg et al. (1978) who first reported this Late
Aptian reversed direction, which is associated with a fossil of narrow range, Planomalina
cheniourensis.
3.3 GORCO A CERBARA SECTION
The Gorgo a Cerbara Section includes the lower part of the Fucoid Marls. Three planktonic
foraminiferal zones are identified in the highest levels sampled at this locality; all are
attributed to the Late Aptian. On the basis of the nannoplankton content the lowermost
part of the Fucoid Marls and the upper levels of the underlying Majolica are also Late Aptian
in age. The Late Aptian Parhabdolithus angustus Zone (Thierstein, 1973) was identified down
to 891.95 m. Sampling in the Gorgo a Cerbara Section continued for about 60 m downwards
into the Majolica. In this interval the age was established on the basis of the nannofossil
content alone. The lowermost part of the P. angustus zone contains the second reversed
polarity zone which is here correlated with anomaly MO (see below). Below the P. angustus
zonal boundary a short interval (from 891.95 to 889.15m) could not be assigned to any
standard zone (all diagnostic forms are missing); it could represent the Lower Aptian. We
saw no evidence for a hiatus. However, if a hiatus exists in this part of the section, this
interval could be the lowermost part of the Upper Aptian.
From 889.15 in down to the base of the usable section at 842.65 in the nannoplankton
assemblage is characterized by Nannoconus colomi and other nannoconids. This assemblage
is indicative of the Barremian Micvantholithus hoschulzi Zone. The Aptian- Barremian
boundary is thus located at about 890 in.
3.4 SUMMARY
The following palaeontological conclusions are of importance in dating the reversal sequence
recognized in the Fucoid Marls and the upper part of the Majolica (and described in the
following sections). The Fucoid Marls cover the interval from the Upper Albian down to the

Upper Aptian. This unit is entirely of normal polarity, with the exception of an ambiguous
reversed zone which was found only in the Valdoria section, where it falls near the top of the
Late Aptian. The Fucoid Marl/Majolica contact falls in the Upper Aptian. The MO reversed
zone probably corresponds to the Lower Aptian, and the other reversed zones encountered
(M1 and M3) fall in the Barremian.
4 Remanent magnetizations
The remanent magnetizations of the 655 specimens were measured with a three-axis ScT
cryogenic magnetometer. Each magnetization was measured twice and the individual com-
ponents of the replicate measurements were combined as described by Heller (1977) so as to
give a synthetic dispersion parameter ($63). In Fig. 3 can be seen how this dispersion
parameter increases as the remanent intensity decreases and the instrumental noise increases.
N =7l4
Rernanent Intensity (Alm)
Figure 3. Variation of the precision parameter $65 with intensity of remanent magnetization in 714
measurements on Lower Cretaceous pelagic carbonate rocks. GISsiss imilar to the angular standard
deviation of repeated measurements and is high when the intensity or quality of the data is low. The
parameter is a useful empirical guide to the reliability of the progressively weakening magnetization at
successive stages of magnetic cleaning.
Large values also result from operator mistakes and the presence of unstable remanence
components whose values alter between the replicate measurements. The value of $63 serves
as a guide to the reliability of each magnetization measurement and can be used as a
quantitative, if somewhat arbitrary, criterion for rejecting poorly determined data. In the
present study all magnetizations weaker than 5 x Am-' or having a $63 value greater
than about 30" were systematically eliminated from further consideration.
The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) is dependent upon the
lithology (Fig. 4). It is greatest in the 'couches rouges' member of the Fucoid Marls, and
drops by about a factor of 50 in the Majolica limestone. Within each of the two lithologies
there is no systematic fluctuation of NRM intensity like that observed in the Scaglia Rossa
and Scaglia Bianca by Alvarez & Lowrie (1978).
Each specimen was demagnetized progressively in peak alternating fields of 5, 10, 15 and
20mT. Additionally, a small number of specimens was demagnetized in higher fields, but
beyond about 40 or 50mT the residual remanences in Majolica specimens became too weak
to measure satisfactorily. The least stable directions and weakest remanences were found in
the Majolica limestone, where a very large low-coercivity magnetization component was
present, and the directional stability was poorer than in the Fucoid Mark (Fig. 5). The grey

member of the Fucoid Mark also had a prominent ‘soft’ component, but after its removal
the direction was fairly stable. The red ‘couches rouges’ samples were more strongly
magnetized and, after removal of an initial large soft component, whose effects were most
pronounced in the negatively magnetized samples, the remanence was stable in intensity and
direction.
Selected specimens were given isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) in progressively
stronger fields. The total coercivity spectrum was deduced by differentiating the IFW
acquisition curves. In specimens of the grey member of the Fucoid Mark (Fig. 6)a nd in
Majolica specimens saturation IRM was reached in fields of less than 0.4 T. Clearly the mag-
netic mineralogy in these pelagic carbonate rocks is dominated by the presence of a magnetic
mineral which is relatively easily saturated and which, by analogy to studies of the Scaglia
limestones (Lowrie 62. Alvarez, 1977b)’ we interpret to be magnetite. In such limestones
there is little reason to suspect that important secondary magnetizations might be present.
This is not the case for the ‘couches rouges’ samples. IRM curves (Fig. 6) have a strong com-
ponent below 0.3 T but are not saturated in fields of 1 T; in addition to magnetite in these
beds we infer that haematite is present, which causes their red colour and may carry an
important secondary magnetization component.
The rate of change of direction was computed at each stage of the demagnetization curve
for each specimen using a method similar to that of Symons & Stupavsky (1974) and the
‘most stable’ direction was selected as the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChFW)
for the specimen. The ChRM directions of specimens from the same sample were compared
for consistency, then combined vectorially to get the mean direction for the sample. Because
of excessive directional inconsistency all specimens from 15 samples were rejected from
further palaeomagnetic analysis.

Samples with exclusively normal ChRM directions were found at the Poggio le Guaine site,
both normal and reversed ChFW directions occurred at the other two locations. The normal
equivalent directions of reversely magnetized samples were used to construct equal area
density stereograms of the ChRM directions before and after AF cleaning, and after making
appropriate tectonic corrections at each location.
The NRM directions (Fig. 7a) are grouped noticeably better than the directions after AF
cleaning. This is due to the presence of a low coercivity component whose direction is close
to that of the present field in Umbria and which probably represents a recent viscous
remanence. This soft component is removed by the AF cleaning, so that the ChRM directions at
first appear to be dispersed (Fig. 7b). They fall into three distinct groups, each corresponding
to a different sampling location; the group of northerly directions come from the Valdorbia

section, the westerly directions are found at Gorgo a Cerbara, and the north-westerly direc-
tions come from Poggio le Guaine. There is not enough variation of bedding attitude within
each section to affect the within-site dispersion of ChRM directions. However, after
correcting for the SW dip of the beds at Valdorbia and the NE dip of the beds at Gorgo a
Cerbara, the directions from these two locations move together into good agreement with

tectonic correction but there are small differences in the declinations of the mean directions
(Table l), which become more noticeable when the data are grouped according to biostrati-
graphic age.
For example, identical average inclinations of 44" are found in the Late Aptian in all
three sections, but the average declinations range from 300 to 325" (Table 2). The Early
Albian mean directions at Poggio le Guaine and Valdorbia also differ mainly in declination.

### page_13
Magnetic stratigraphy in carbonate rocks 275
The declinations in the Albian and Late Aptian Fucoid Marls are distinctly larger than the
westward declinations in the Early Aptian and Barremian Majolica limestone (Tables 1 and 2).
After rotating the pole of the stereogram to the mean direction of Fig. 7c, the distribution
is found to be approximately elliptical with an axial ratio of about 1.5 : 1. As a result the
tectonicallycorrected ChRM directions in Fig. 7c appear more smeared in declination than
in inclination. At least three factors may contribute to this elongation of the combined
directional distribution. Firstly, intermediate directions at all three locations, especially at
reversal boundaries, have not been removed. Secondly, the mean ages of the samples are
slightly different at each section. Poggio le Guaine and Valdorbia samples are Albian and
Late Aptian in age and Gorgo a Cerbara samples are Aptian and Barremian. The difference
between the mean directions of the sections (Table 1) may result from polar wander from
the Barremian through the Albian; little is known about geomagnetic field behaviour during
these Early Cretaceous stages, but the observed trend is compatible with expectations based
on either the African or European polar wander path of Van der Voo & French (1 9 74).
The third factor which could contribute to the smearing of directions in Fig. 7c is
incorrectness of the tectonic corrections. The beds at each site were restored to the horizon-
tal by assuming that they had been folded simply about a horizontal axis. Although the
folding of the Umbrian Apennines appears at first to be simple, the tectonic style may
actually be more complex than hitherto suspected (Alvarez, Engelder & Geiser 1978).
Considerable divergence of palaeomagnetic directions throughout Umbria may be related to
local variation in fold axis attitude (Channell et al. 1978) and may account for distinct
differences in declination between long sections that are less than 20 km apart (Alvarez &
Lowrie 1978).
The positive response to the tectonic fold test indicates that ChRM directions in the Fucoid
Mark and Majolica limestone predate the Late Tertiary folding of the Umbrian Apennines.
The dominance of magnetite in the grey member of the Fucoid Mark and in the Majolica
argue in favour of a depositional (or immediately post-depositional) origin for the remanent
magnetization, as found in the Scaglia Rossa and Scaglia Bianca pelagic limestones elsewhere
in Umbria (Lowrie & Alvarez 1975, 1977b). It is therefore permissible to associate the
remanent magnetizations with their stratigraphic positions, although the effect of hematite
in the ‘couches rouges’ samples must be considered in more detail.
5 Magnetic stratigraphy
The declinations and inclinations of tectonically corrected ChRM directions showed a
systematic relationship to stratigraphic position (Fig. 8). All Poggio le Guaine samples were
normally magnetized, and there was no appreciable difference of directions between grey
member and ‘couches rouges’ member samples. A clearly indicated reversal in the ‘couches
rouges’ member at Valdorbia is marked by simultaneous inversion of both declinations and
inclinations. The reversed directions are not exactly antipodal to the normal samples; the
angular difference between the mean directions of the two groups is 130”. It is probable
that a stable secondary magnetization has not been removed by the AF cleaning. This
reversal corresponds to the reversely magnetized ISEA site of VandenBerg et al. (1978).
No corresponding reversed interval is found in the ‘couches rouges’ samples from the other
sections, but several synchronous inversions of declination and inclination are present in
the Majolica in the Gorgo a Cerbara section.
The latitude of the virtual geomagnetic pole (VCP) relative to the sampling sites at the
time of deposition is used as a clearer indicator of geomagnetic polarity. The inclination of

of the three sections (Fig. 2) so as to date each of the polarity reversals. No reversals are
found in the Albian, two occur in the Aptian, and several are found in the Barremian. Further
interpretation of these reversals requires a clearer understanding of the nature of the ISEA
reversed polarity zone.
6 The Valdorbia Reversal (ISEA)
The directions of magnetization in red ‘couches rouges’ samples at Poggio le Guaine and
Gorgo a Cerbara were normal, whereas those in four adjacent ‘couches rouges’ beds at
Valdorbia were reversed. The absence of reversals in the first two sections may imply that the
indurated beds were not originally deposited synchronously. The IRM acquisition tests
suggest the presence of both magnetite and haematite in ‘couches rouges’ samples. There-
fore, after demagnetizing them to 25 mT, the Valdorbia reversely magnetized samples were
further demagnetized by stepwise progressive thermal demagnetization.
Demagnetization data obtained from pelagic limestones are usually of sufficiently good
quality to permit analysis of directional variation. Consistency of directions or directional
trends can usually be established before signals become too weak or unstable to measure
accurately. In samples from their reversed site ISEA VandenBerg et al. (1978) established
two distinct components of remanence. A component between 0.1 1 and 0.3 T was identified
as the primary component; the lower coercivity component could not be identified. In our
samples from the Valdorbia section the following characteristics are clearly established (Fig.
10): (I) a large directional change occurs during AF demagnetization to 10 mT, accompanying
removal of a normal overprint; (2) the directions at 15 and 25 mT are stable and their mean
M
Figure 10. Variation of the mean direction of 10 reversely magnetized samples from the reversal in the
Valdorbia section, prior to tectonic corrections. All directions are on the lower hemisphere; numbers
5-25 give the peak AF demagnetizing field in millitesla; numbers 300-500 identify the temperature eC)
to which the samples were heated in subsequent thermal demagnetization. The bars on each point define
the orthogonal diameters of the 95 per cent confidence circle. The directions after thermal demagnetization
in the 300-500°C range are indistinguishable from those after 20 and 25 mT AF demagnetization; all

### page_16
2 78 W.L owrie et al.
has declination 188”, inclination -14”; (3) during further thermal demagnetization the
directions remain quite stable and over the range 300-500’C the mean direction has
declination 184”, inclination -1 2’; (4) accurate measurements were not possible after heating
to 600°C, because the remanences became at the same time weak and unstable, and were
randomly directed.
We interpret from these results that the magnetite and haematite components in the
Valdorbia samples have essentially the same stable directions, and that this corresponds to
reversed polarity.’
It is unlikely that the haematite formed long after deposition. The next confirmed geo-
magnetic reversal after deposition of the Valdorbia sediment corresponds to the negative
Gubbio A-zone (Alvarez et al. 1977) which occurred more than 30 Myr later, by which time
the sediment was buried to a depth of more than 300 m. In order to be negatively magnetized
like the magnetite fraction the ‘couches rouges’ haematization probably occurred fairly soon
after deposition as a result of the decomposition of goethite during diagenesis. It is not greatly
erroneous to associate the reversal in the Valdorbia ‘couches rouges’ beds with the strati-
graphic level at which it is found.
7 Discussions
Correlation of magnetic stratigraphies from one section to another, or correlation of the
magnetic stratigraphy derived in a sedimentary section with the geomagnetic polarity
sequence deduced from oceanic anomalies, is only possible when the record possesses a
distinctive character, or ‘fingerprint’. Otherwise, the cross-correlation of similar binary
sequences presents unresolvable ambiguity. The appearance of the ‘fingerprint’ can be
drastically altered by non-uniformity of sedimentation rate and/or sea-floor spreading rate.
The magnetic reversal history of the Late Cretaceous between anomalies 34 and 29 contained
alternating polarity zones of variable duration, and correlation of the magnetic stratigraphies
in the Gubbio and Moria sections (Alvarez & Lowrie, 1978) and to the oceanic anomaly
sequence (Lowrie & Alvarez, 1977a,b) was unmistakable. The oceanic equivalent to
the Lower Cretaceous magnetic stratigraphy defined in the present study is to be found
among the youngest anomalies of the Mesozoic sequence (Larson & Hilde 1975). The
geomagnetic polarity pattern for anomalies MO to M4 offers a suitable ‘fingerprint’ for
correlation with the polarity sequence in Fig. 9.
The oldest reversal found in the Gubbio and Moria sections corresponded to anomaly 24,
and occurred very near to the Santonian-Campanian boundary. The Santonian, Coniacian,
Turonian and Cenomanian stages all belong to the Cretaceous magnetic quiet interval. From
the present study there is no evidence of reversals in the Albian, and we infer that this stage
also belongs to the quiet interval.
If the Valdorbia reversal ISEA is assumed to be a synsedimentary record of a Late Aptian
geomagnetic reversal, the magnetic stratigraphy in the Lower Cretaceous pelagic carbonate
rocks contains evidence for at least one extra reversal that has not been identified in the
Mesozoic sequence. Two possible correlations of our data with the MO to M4 anomaly
sequence may then be suggested (Fig. 1 1). In correlation A the Valdorbia reversal is equated
with the reversed zone that produces anomaly MO, and by implication the unidentified
reversal lies between MO and MI. It is, however, unlikely that such a prominent reversal would
be overlooked in interpreting the oceanic anomalies. The correlation B has less distorted tie-
line and identifies anomaly MO with the Early Aptian; according to this correlation the
Valdorbia reversal is an unidentified Late Aptian event. If the Valdorbia reversal is in fact a

8 Conclusions
The magnetic stratigraphies from the Upper Cretaceous Scaglia limestones at Gubbio and
Moria are combined with those from the Lower Cretaceous Fucoid Marl and Majolica lime-
stone sections in the present study to give a composite geomagnetic polarity sequence for
the Barremian through Maastrichtian stages. This sequence is in good agreement with the
geomagnetic polarity history of the Cretaceous as derived from oceanic magnetic anomalies
(Fig. 12). According to this correlation anomaly MO is of Early Aptian age, which agrees
with the identification and dating of this anomaly in the Biancone limestone by Channell et
al. (1979). These data imply that the Cretaceous magnetic quiet zone began earlier, ended
later and consequently was of longer duration than has been assumed from interpretation of
oceanic magnetic anomalies.
The identification of the Valdorbia reversal as a real geomagnetic phenomenon contem-
poraneous with deposition of the ‘couches rouges’beds rests largely on rock magnetic grounds
and is not entirely satisfactory. The reversal was not found in the ‘couches rouges’ member
in the other sections, despite intensive re-sampling of all available beds. It is possible that the
indurated beds are not time-equivalent in the different sections. Nevertheless, the reversal is
